Learned methods can search high-dimensional spaces faster than a designer can enumerate them, fit empirical patterns where no analytical model is available, and propose candidate structures a designer would not have drafted. Applying those capabilities to computer systems and silicon chip design is one of the most unforgiving tests they face. An architectural decision begins with high-level software intent and cascades through compilers, instruction set architectures (ISAs), microarchitectures, and register-transfer level (RTL) netlists down to physical silicon signoff. Along this path, empirical observations are expensive, noisy, and inherently partial. Compilers, cycle-level simulators, formal verification engines, and post-layout timing tools each expose a narrow slice of system behavior under conflicting assumptions. Worse still, the cost of error in hardware is asymmetric: while software can be patched in production, a timing glitch or coherence bug discovered after mask tapeout costs tens of millions of dollars and months of schedule delay.

That asymmetric penalty defines both the danger and the opportunity of automated design. Generative models can draft candidate RTL and architectural variations far faster than physical toolchains can evaluate them. But proposing alternatives creates engineering value only when the system can qualify what those alternatives physically achieve. An *AI-native design system* does not bolt machine-learning models onto existing scripts; it rebuilds the exploration loop around the tools that return evidence. It unites learned surrogates, deterministic simulators, and physical signoff engines around machine-usable state representations, co-designing hardware and software under a verification budget.

The ambition of this book extends past generating Verilog from natural-language prompts or training standalone performance predictors. The question is whether a complete, closed-loop design system can find better architectures, reduce the engineering cost of finding them, or do both. I wrote this book to make that possibility concrete without assuming its success. The chapters establish the principles, state representations, and execution harnesses required to pursue the moonshot without mistaking local code generation for full-system success.

The architectural problem always comes first. Depending on the physical constraints, the right engineering choice may combine learned surrogates, heuristic optimization, formal proofs, or conventional analysis with no machine learning at all. Architecture 2.0 is not a dogma claiming that every circuit demands an AI model; it is a discipline for determining where AI earns its place and what physical evidence its recommendations must deliver.

## On the Title of This Book {.unnumbered}

The title of this book, *Architecture 2.0: Principles of AI-Native System and Chip Design*, is a compact declaration of its scope, where each term establishes a deliberate boundary. Architecture 2.0 names a shift in how architecture work is done,[^fn-paradigm-shift-c00] which this book defends rather than takes on faith: the transition from manual, intuition-driven point sweeps toward automated, closed-loop exploration across the full hardware–software stack. I chose *Principles* because specific model weights and tool scripts are transient, whereas the underlying physics, evidence standards, and architectural trade-offs outlast them.

[^fn-paradigm-shift-c00]: **Author's note**: I do not use the term *paradigm shift* lightly. In the classic formulation of @Kuhn1962ScientificRevolutions, a paradigm shift occurs when a discipline's established methods encounter physical and operational limits that incremental adjustments can no longer resolve. I argue that computer systems design has reached that inflection point, and this book establishes the empirical evidence standards by which that claim must be judged.

*AI-native* carries a precise technical meaning in this work. Point AI assistance retrofits a standalone model onto an isolated computer-aided design (CAD) task while leaving the manual, error-prone engineering handoffs untouched. An AI-native design system, by contrast, constructs the entire exploration workflow, state representations, and verification harnesses around automated search and multi-tool orchestration. Finally, *System and Chip Design* names the physical reality that a silicon floorplan cannot be optimized in isolation from the software workloads, compiler lowering passes, memory hierarchies, and thermal constraints that govern its behavior.

## What This Book Teaches {.unnumbered}

This book traces an architectural hypothesis through the evidence an engineering claim requires. Architects formulate the governing question, construct a machine-usable representation of design state, choose methods, and execute deterministic tools to evaluate proposed candidates. What the tools return must then be interpreted causally, compared against credible baselines at matched cost, and distilled into a technical recommendation that a named authority can defend. The focus stays on the physical mechanisms and trade-offs that architects must judge rather than on the transient syntax of any individual tool.

Evaluating whether an automated workflow improves a design program requires scrutinizing the entire human-and-tool system. A fluent generative model inside a broken verification loop accelerates the production of invalid silicon. Conversely, a modest, well-calibrated surrogate that eliminates a weeks-long simulation bottleneck can change a tapeout schedule. Every method in this book faces two questions. *Did the complete approach improve the architecture result, or reduce the total cost of reaching a comparable one, against a credible alternative?* And *should a named authority commit physical silicon to the result?* The first question is technical and measurable. The second is an organizational judgment that a person makes and owns.

Answering those questions means moving past isolated point tools to govern the whole exploration life cycle. The reader learns to formulate the question and represent the design state, to connect methods to real tools and qualify what those tools return, and to evaluate the complete approach and own the commitment that follows.

To keep these principles grounded in silicon, the text develops a recurring Lighthouse case study: a real-time mobile extended-reality (XR) compute subsystem operating under a strict 3\ W thermal design power (TDP) budget and tight silicon area constraints. The Lighthouse study opens with intent formulation in @sec-moonshot, formalizes state representations and tool interfaces in @sec-data-representations-world-models and @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces, runs a cycle-level accelerator array study in @sec-running-the-loop and stops where its record stops, and returns in @sec-what-architect-owns to state what those results do and do not justify. Nothing in this subsystem can be settled in isolation. The power envelope constrains the accelerator, the accelerator reshapes memory traffic, and the memory hierarchy shifts thermal hot spots across the die. Holding the Lighthouse study to the same admission criteria the book asks of the field is how it shows what an honest stop looks like, with unresolved risks kept as open questions rather than claimed as victories.

Architecture 2.0 sits at the intersection of computer architecture, machine learning, and electronic design automation (@fig-book-composition). Each overlap already has a field of work behind it. Architecture and machine learning help us predict performance and search large design spaces. Architecture and electronic design automation (EDA) connect system choices to RTL and physical implementation. Machine learning and EDA are already changing synthesis, placement, routing, and verification. What we are after sits where all three meet.

![**Architecture 2.0 unifies computer architecture, machine learning, and EDA.** Computer architecture supplies the questions and design trade-offs, machine learning supplies methods for learning and search, and EDA supplies executable implementation and analysis tools together with physical evidence or estimates. Work at their intersection must satisfy the relevant standards of all three.](images/fig-book-composition){#fig-book-composition width="100%" fig-alt="Three-circle Venn diagram of computer architecture, machine learning, and electronic design automation, with Architecture 2.0 at their intersection"}

Work at that intersection has to satisfy all three fields at once. A generated artifact that ignores the workload is not an architecture result. A promising estimate that cannot survive implementation is not a physical result. A successful tool run without a fair comparison does not show that AI improved the work.

The book distinguishes three ways machine learning enters hardware design: point assistance inside an established workflow, bounded optimization of a subsystem whose interfaces stay fixed, and AI-native design systems that structure the whole exploration workflow around closed-loop search under human commitment authority. @sec-moonshot defines the three and explains why the distinction matters; much published work lives in the first two, and the moonshot of Architecture 2.0 is the third carried all the way to physically verified silicon. This book is not a catalog of transient neural architectures, a prompt-engineering recipe, or a defense of unconstrained automation. I do not argue that heuristics should replace architectural judgment or formal verification. Physical signoff checks remain decisive, and named human architects remain accountable for every committed gate.

## The Discipline of Design Principles {.unnumbered}

Machine-learning models and EDA scripts change every month, and the prompts and software wrappers written for them go stale with them. What lasts is a principle rooted in semiconductor physics, in the cost of a measurement, and in a documented failure. The test I applied to each candidate principle is whether it would still govern the silicon outcome if model capability grew by orders of magnitude and inference cost fell to zero; a rule that fails that test describes a tool, not the discipline.

The principles appear where the argument earns them. Each chapter states its own as a callout, and each part page lists the principles its chapters carry. @sec-appendix-c-design-principles collects the eight core principles those chapter rules instantiate, each with the failure it predicts, the review question that makes it inspectable, and the boundary beyond which it stops applying, and maps every chapter principle to its core. The companion @sec-appendix-c-laws-paradoxes gathers the borrowed laws and paradoxes the chapters invoke, from Amdahl's law to the optimizer's curse, so a reader can find a derivation without rereading the chapter that used it.

## Who This Book Is For {.unnumbered}

The primary audience is the practicing computer architect, chip designer, and systems researcher. I assume familiarity with performance, power, area, and hardware–software interfaces, alongside working literacy in engineering software (Python, C++, or standard hardware description languages). No prior background in deep learning is required; the machine-learning ideas the argument needs are introduced where they are used, through concrete architecture problems and physical constraints.

Because Architecture 2.0 bridges traditionally isolated silos, the text addresses four technical communities:

- **Computer architects** seeking to integrate automated search and generative models into design exploration without loosening the physical checks that make a result trustworthy.
- **EDA and CAD engineers** looking to connect synthesis, placement, and verification toolchains to high-level architectural decision loops.
- **Machine learning and ML-systems researchers** entering hardware design who need to understand how physical signoff, evaluation costs, and formal verification redefine what constitutes a valid result.
- **Graduate students and engineering leaders** spanning hardware and software who need a framework and a shared vocabulary for governing AI-native systems engineering.

## How to Read This Book {#book-structure .unnumbered}

This book is organized into four cumulative parts that follow an architectural study from initial intent to physical signoff and organizational commitment:

- **Part I: System Intent and Design Life Cycles** analyzes the physical scaling limits and economic pressures breaking manual design loops and introduces the six-stage design life cycle (Formulate, Explore, Implement, Evaluate, Interpret, and Commit), grounded in the running Lighthouse mobile XR moonshot.
- **Part II: Technical Building Blocks** constructs the engineering infrastructure of Architecture 2.0: structured state representations, smallest sufficient methods, isolated tool harnesses, and the qualification of returned signals before they drive any action.
- **Part III: Closed-Loop Execution and Ownership** runs a design study as far as its execution records reach and reports where execution stops, analyzes cross-stack pattern transfer, applies adversarial red-teaming and matched-budget evaluation, and establishes nondelegable human commitment authority.
- **Part IV: Open Infrastructure and Ecosystems** charts the precompetitive schemas, open process design kits (PDKs), grand challenges, and university curricula needed to sustain an open research ecosystem.

Reading sequentially gives the complete engineering argument, and each of the four communities above can also enter through the chapters closest to its own work (@tbl-reading-paths). Three chapters form the spine every path shares: the moonshot and its evidence standard (@sec-moonshot), the life cycle that organizes the work (@sec-architecture-20-ontology), and the commitment decision that ends it (@sec-what-architect-owns).

| **Reader** | **Start with** | **Then** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |

| EDA and CAD engineer | @sec-data-representations-world-models, @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces | @sec-feedback-verification-trust, @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack |

Every path passes through the moonshot, the life cycle, and the commitment decision. {#tbl-reading-paths tbl-colwidths="[24,38,38]"}

As you read, test these principles against a live design problem in your own work. Ask which decision matters, what hidden physical constraints must be exposed, which baseline comparison is fair, what the tools actually measured, and what risks remain unverified. The measure of this book is whether its principles carry to design problems it never mentions.

Specific neural architectures, benchmark leaderboards, and EDA tool APIs will continue to change. The reasoning in this book is built to outlast them. A team that grounds its automated design work in problem formulation, explicit state representation, tool discipline, adversarial evaluation, and human commitment authority can adopt new models without rebuilding its method each time.

I expect artificial intelligence to change how architects design chips and systems. Whether it does depends on the discipline taking that prospect seriously without taking anyone's claims on faith, mine included. Generating code is not that change. The change, if it comes, will come from design systems that carry intent to checked physical results and from architects with the judgment to govern them. Architecture 2.0 is the discipline for deciding where AI belongs, where it does not, and what the evidence shows.
